title: Xueyan Feng
text:
I study how people judge messages when AI takes part in writing or selecting them. My research asks how AI involvement changes what a message signals about its sender, and which messages reach the public.
I am a master’s student in Integrated Marketing Communications at Northwestern University (M.S. expected December 2026). My current projects look at how large language models (LLMs) recommend brands, how restaurants’ replies to online reviews changed after ChatGPT, and how AI note writers affect what X’s Community Notes publishes. I hold a B.A. in Korean Language and Literature from Peking University.
Research interests: AI-mediated communication · gatekeeping on platforms and by AI · computational communication

title: Research
text: Generative AI now writes messages matched to a recipient at minimal human effort, and it increasingly helps decide which messages people read. My projects take up both sides of this change: what a message still signals about its sender when AI helps write it, and how AI changes gatekeeping, the process that reduces countless pieces of information to the few messages that reach the public.

title: Research
text:
What AI-assisted messages signal

Accommodation made cheap: AI and restaurants’ replies to online reviews


Question

How did restaurants’ public replies to online reviews change after ChatGPT, and does tailoring a reply to the review still set it apart?

Theory

Communication accommodation theory; signaling theory

Data

8.9 million reviews and 487,906 replies on OpenTable across six U.S. metro areas

Methods

Interrupted time series with restaurant and period fixed effects; tailoring measured as how closely a reply resembles the review it answers

Findings

Compared with before 2023, replies took up their reviews far more closely, most of all in quarters when AI likely wrote at least half of a restaurant’s replies. More tailored replies went with more later reviews before 2023 but no longer did from 2023. The data cannot yet attribute that change to AI authorship.

Status

Extended abstract submitted to ICA 2027

section: Gatekeeping on platforms and by AI
text:
Gatekeeping on platforms and by AI

Diminishing returns to AI note writers: Human raters limit what Community Notes publish


Question

Do AI note writers increase what X’s Community Notes publishes? AI programs can write notes, but only humans rate them, and a note is published only when raters with differing perspectives rate it helpful.

Theory

Gatekeeping theory

Data

791,143 notes flagging posts as misleading, September 2025 to September 2026

Methods

Time-series and fixed-effects models

Findings

Ratings tracked human-written notes, not AI-written ones. When AI output doubled, each AI note received 10% fewer ratings and was 12% less likely to be published. AI writers scaled up note production far more than the human ratings that decide which notes are published.

Status

First-author extended abstract submitted to ICA 2027





The Silent Gatekeeper: Brand visibility in LLM recommendations


Question

How often and how prominently do large language models (LLMs) recommend brands to consumers seeking product advice? The study treats LLMs as gatekeepers between consumers and brands.

Data

Repeated queries to multiple LLMs through their APIs, each in a new session with no conversation history; five product categories; needs-based prompts

Methods

Brand Recommendation Probability for how often a brand is recommended, and an adapted Mean Reciprocal Rank for how prominently; regularized regression on marketplace-visibility measures

Findings

Many major brands were rarely or never recommended. Recommendation prominence was associated with marketplace visibility, particularly search interest and online brand conversation.

Status

Revise and resubmit, Journal of Advertising Research. A related paper is submitted to ECIR 2027 (arXiv:2609.16304).





The machine brand image: Evaluating LLM recommendations across prompts and models


Question

What do LLMs say about the brands they recommend? The study treats these justifications as brand associations.

Theory

Brand-knowledge framework (Keller)

Data

17,821 justifications from six LLMs across five product categories

Methods

Coding into eight association types, linked to marketplace data

Findings

The associations mirrored brands’ positioning and were largely shared across LLMs. A consumer’s stated need shifted them from reputation toward situational fit.

Status

Competitive paper accepted at AAA 2027; submitted to Journal of Advertising





How an LLM’s knowledge of the consumer shapes brand recommendations


Question

How does an LLM’s knowledge of the consumer shape its brand recommendations?

Design

Compares a stateless model, the user’s own LLM personalization, and a synthetic persona, with participants querying their own AI assistants

My role

Designed the participant survey and ran the factor analysis

Status

Paper in preparation for ICORIA 2027
